telescope.name: Celestron NexStar 127 SLT (Maksutov-Cassegrain)
telescope.mount: NexStar SLT computerised alt-azimuth (single fork arm)

cameras.name: ZWO ASI585MC (uncooled)

priceRef.usedNote: typical used asking prices — the live listings below are the real figure

strengths: 2.9 µm pixels are almost perfectly matched to f/12 for planets — no Barlow needed in average UK seeing
Very low read noise (≈0.8 e⁻ at high gain) makes 2–10 s stacked sub-exposures far more efficient than with a DSLR
Larger 4K chip than the 662: frames M81, M51, M57, M27, M13 and the core of M42
Live stacking in SharpCap/ASIStudio aligns and de-rotates frames, which suits an alt-az mount
weaknesses: Needs a laptop and USB 3 cable at the scope
At 1,500 mm the field (≈26′ × 14′) only shows the core of M42
Has a clear AR window, so you need a UV/IR-cut filter for natural colour
cameras.adapters: Comes with a 1.25″ nosepiece. Remove the star diagonal and push it straight into the 127 SLT visual back. Screw a 1.25″ UV/IR-cut filter into the nosepiece. Optional 0.5× 1.25″ reducer for deep sky.

cameras.name: ZWO ASI662MC
strengths: Same pixel size and per-pixel performance as the 585 for half the price
Fast frame rates (100+ fps at small ROI) freeze UK seeing for Jupiter and Saturn
No amp glow and very low read noise
weaknesses: Tiny 12.8′ × 7.3′ field at 1,500 mm: only small deep-sky targets fit (M57, the M27 core, the M13 core)
Needs a UV/IR-cut filter
cameras.adapters: Supplied 1.25″ nosepiece goes into the visual back, with the diagonal removed. Add a 1.25″ UV/IR-cut filter.

cameras.name: Canon EOS 600D / 650D / 700D (used)
cameras.badge: Best budget pick — frames most of M42

priceRef.usedNote: MPB UK 600D listings seen 17 Oct 2026 (£108–£179, with 12-month warranty)

strengths: APS-C field (≈51′ × 34′) shows the whole bright part of M42 at prime focus
The 600D's 640×480 movie-crop mode gives usable planetary video with a 2× Barlow
Fully supported by BackyardEOS, APT, N.I.N.A. and DeepSkyStacker; you can later move it to a camera lens or tracker for M31
Cheapest way to start, with no laptop needed (use an intervalometer)
weaknesses: Read noise ≈3 e⁻ hurts on 5 s subs, so you need more frames than with a ZWO camera
Stock IR filter cuts most H-alpha. M42 still looks great, but faint red nebulae suffer
Weight (≈550 g) on a 1.25″ nosepiece strains the SLT's fork arm. Balance it and go gently with the slews
cameras.adapters: Canon EF T-ring plus a 1.25″ T-mount nosepiece, pushed into the visual back with the diagonal removed. For planets, put the 2× Barlow in the visual back and the nosepiece into the Barlow.

cameras.name: Nikon D5300 (used)

sensor.model: Sony-made APS-C 24 MP, no AA filter

priceRef.usedNote: typical used range (unverified). Check the live listings

strengths: Lower read noise and better dynamic range than the 600D, a popular astro body on Stargazers Lounge
Same APS-C framing advantage for M42
Has an articulating screen, which helps at the back of a Mak pointed high
weaknesses: Weaker astro software support than Canon (tethering and bulb control are more fiddly)
No planetary crop mode, so it is poor for Jupiter and Saturn video
Has no intervalometer port of the Canon type: you need a Nikon remote or an app
cameras.adapters: Nikon F T-ring plus a 1.25″ T-mount nosepiece into the visual back.

cameras.name: ZWO ASI224MC (used)

priceRef.usedNote: typical used range — largely superseded by the 662

strengths: Proven planetary camera. A Mak 127 with a 2× Barlow lands near its ideal ≈f/19–20
Low read noise and high frame rate
Cheap second-hand and a good guide camera later
weaknesses: Very small 1.2 MP chip that is of little use for deep sky at 1,500 mm
Older sensor with some amp glow. A new 662 is better for about £60 more
cameras.adapters: 1.25″ nosepiece (usually included) into the visual back, or into the 2× Barlow.

cameras.name: ZWO ASI678MC
strengths: 8 MP gives lovely lunar mosaics and closely framed planets
Lowest read noise of the group
weaknesses: 2 µm pixels are already oversampled at f/12 (ideal ≈f/10), so the Barlow is never needed
For deep sky, 0.28″/px is wasted at 1,500 mm and you must bin 2×2. The 585 is the better buy
cameras.adapters: Supplied 1.25″ nosepiece into the visual back, plus a UV/IR-cut filter.

cameras.name: Canon EOS RP (used, full-frame mirrorless)
cameras.badge: Only if you also want a daytime camera

priceRef.usedNote: typical used range (unverified). Check the live listings

strengths: Closest thing to the R6 Mark II you borrowed: full-frame, a great live view for focusing, and RF-mount T-rings available
A superb general and wide-field astro camera with lenses
weaknesses: The Mak's baffle tube vignettes a full-frame sensor heavily at prime focus
Costs 3–4× more than a 600D for little gain on this telescope
Big 5.7 µm pixels need ≈f/28 for planets
cameras.adapters: Canon RF T-ring (or EF T-ring plus Canon EF-RF adapter) plus a 1.25″ nosepiece. A 2″ path is not available on the 127 SLT.

cameras.name: ZWO ASI533MC Pro (cooled)
cameras.badge: Not worth it on the SLT mount
strengths: Superb deep-sky camera on an equatorial mount with 60–300 s guided subs
Square chip, no amp glow, set-point cooling for matching darks
weaknesses: Cooling only pays off on long exposures. With 2–8 s subs on an alt-az mount, dark current is already negligible
Too slow and the wrong pixel size for planets
Costs more than a Star Adventurer GTi, which would help you far more
cameras.adapters: M42 front thread plus a 1.25″ nosepiece. It also needs a 12 V supply for the cooler.
